title: Given the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer `k`, reverse every consecutive group of `k` nodes in place and return the new head. If the final group has fewer than `k` nodes, leave it as is. Use O(1) extra space.
shortTitle: Reverse every K-element Sub-list (Reverse Nodes in Groups of K)

s1_definition.profdef: Iterate the list group by group. For each full group of `k` nodes, reverse those `k` nodes with the three-pointer technique and re-stitch the reversed group between the tail of the previous group and the head of the next group. Stop reversing when fewer than `k` nodes remain.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India batches settlement slips into fixed bundles of k. Each bundle must be read in reverse, but the bundles stay in their overall order. The clerk flips each bundle of k slips in place, keeping the bundles themselves in sequence, and leaves a final short bundle untouched.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reverse each full k-node group and re-link group boundaries; leave a trailing partial group alone.

sections.s3_flow:
```
  Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5   (k=2)
    │
    ▼
  SettlementBundler.reverseInGroups()
    │ group[1,2] → 2 -> 1 ; previousTail=node1
    │ group[3,4] → 4 -> 3 ; previousTail=node3
    │ remaining [5] < k → leave
    ▼
  Output: 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 5
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a linked list in groups of k is the three-pointer reversal applied repeatedly, and the whole difficulty is the bookkeeping that stitches the groups together rather than the reversal itself. I keep a previous-tail pointer, starting at a dummy before the head, which after each reversed group points to that group's new tail, namely the group's original first node. For each group I first count ahead to confirm k nodes remain; if fewer remain I stop and leave that short tail group in its natural order.

When a full group exists I reverse exactly k nodes with the usual three pointers, then reconnect three links: the previous tail points to the group's new head, the group's original first node points to the start of the next group, and I advance the previous tail to that original first node for the next round. All of this is one forward pass in constant space, and I prefer it over the recursive form because recursion would consume stack proportional to the number of groups.

In my work at the National Bank of India this backed a batch slip printer that printed settlement slips in fixed bundles of k, each bundle reversed internally while the bundles stayed in sequence, with a final short bundle printed normally. Flipping each full bundle in place and carefully relinking the bundle boundaries produced exactly that ordering without building a second chain.

Remember one sentence: understand the core algorithm and apply it to banking domain problems.
